To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Engel curves are not only upward sloping but also convex and, in addition, that the income elasticity of demand is not a constant but a function of income.

the Engel curve for food is flatter than the Engel curve for non food, that Engel curves of non food categories exhibit a variety of income elasticities, that the income elasticity of demand of non food is higher than that of food, that the income elasticities of non food categories are not equal, and that Engel curves for non food categories are steeper than the Engel curve of food.
Engel curves for necessities have a lower income elasticity of demand, and thus a lower slope than Engel curves for luxuries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether and how Engel’s law can be extended to welfare analysis.
the development of Engel curves and the implications of the Engel curves for poverty analysis.
the question whether the income elasticity of demand can be used as a measure for the welfare impact of rising income.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in general, food expenditure decreases with rising income.
Engel curves are not only a function of income but also of a number of socio-demographic characteristics, such as household size, household composition and age.
the Engel curves of the expenditure categories of food and non-food are not parallel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Engel’s law is not a law at all but a pattern of human behavior that can be observed across countries and across time.
Engel’s legacy is still alive and well.
the Engel curve is a powerful tool for analyzing the structure of consumer behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Engel’s law is a necessary but insufficient condition for welfare.
the income elasticity of demand for necessities is significantly higher in developing countries than in developed countries.
the Engelian approach to welfare is still valid and can be used as an alternative to conventional poverty measures, which do not consider the behavioral aspects of consumer expenditure.
